nameStory: The Brown Centipede gets its straightforward name from its rich brown coloration that helps it blend perfectly with soil and leaf litter. It's also called the 'garden centipede' because it's so commonly found scurrying around in garden beds, and 'stone centipede' for its habit of hiding under rocks during the day.
description: The Brown Centipede is a fast-moving predator with a flattened, segmented body that's typically reddish-brown to dark brown in color. These arthropods have exactly 15 pairs of long, spindly legs that give them their characteristic quick, undulating movement. They usually measure about 1-2 inches long and have a pair of venomous claws near their head for capturing prey like small insects and spiders. Despite their fearsome appearance, they're actually beneficial creatures that help control garden pests.

idTips.label: Leg Count
idTips.description: Always has exactly 15 pairs of legs (30 total) - count carefully as this distinguishes centipedes from millipedes which have many more pairs per segment

idTips.label: Body Shape
idTips.description: Flattened body that feels firm but flexible when gently handled, with distinct segments visible along its length

idTips.label: Color Pattern
idTips.description: Rich brown to reddish-brown coloration with slightly darker bands across each segment, giving it a striped appearance

idTips.label: Movement Style
idTips.description: Moves in a distinctive serpentine wave pattern when running, with legs creating a rippling motion along its sides

idTips.label: Antennae
idTips.description: Long, thread-like antennae that are constantly moving and feeling ahead as it explores - about half the length of its body

idTips.label: Head Features
idTips.description: Large, prominent head with visible jaw-like claws (forcipules) that curve forward like pincers

habitat: Look for Brown Centipedes in moist areas throughout New England, especially under logs, stones, mulch, and leaf litter in gardens, forests, and wooded areas. They prefer the cool, damp conditions found in basements, crawl spaces, and around building foundations. You'll often find them in compost piles and under potted plants where the soil stays consistently moist.

seasonality.spring: Most active as temperatures warm up, often seen hunting at night or discovered when turning over garden stones and logs. This is when they emerge from deeper winter hiding spots.
seasonality.summer: Peak activity season - frequently spotted in gardens during evening watering or when disturbing mulch. Hot, dry weather may drive them to seek shelter in basements and cool, damp areas.
seasonality.fall: Still quite active but beginning to seek deeper shelter for winter. Often found when cleaning up garden beds or moving firewood.
seasonality.winter: Much less active and hidden deep under logs, stones, or in basement cracks. Occasionally seen in heated buildings where they remain somewhat active.

funFact: Brown Centipedes are actually deaf and nearly blind, navigating their world almost entirely through touch and chemical signals - yet they're such skilled hunters they can catch flying insects right out of the air using only their sense of vibration!
confusionNotes: Often confused with millipedes, but remember: centipedes are fast and fierce (one pair of legs per segment), while millipedes are slow and shy (two pairs of legs per segment). Memory trick: 'Centipede' sounds like 'century' (100) - fewer legs, faster movement!
contextualKnowledge: Despite the name 'centipede' meaning '100 feet,' no centipede actually has 100 legs - they always have an odd number of leg pairs. The Brown Centipede's scientific name 'forficatus' means 'forked' or 'scissor-like,' referring to its prominent jaw claws.
compareHints: The Brown Centipede is larger and more robust than its relatives the Garden Lithobius and Least Lithobius. Garden Lithobius tends to be slightly smaller with more subdued coloring, while Least Lithobius is notably smaller and paler. Brown Centipedes also have more prominent, darker banding across their segments compared to their plainer-colored cousins.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Garden Lithobius is distinguished from the Brown Centipede by its reddish-brown coloration and slightly smaller size, while the Least Lithobius is much smaller overall.
The Least Lithobius is significantly smaller and more delicate than its relatives the Brown Centipede and Garden Lithobius, which can grow much larger and have more robust builds.
